nameStory: The pink-edged sulphur gets its name from the delicate rosy-pink border that outlines its wings, particularly visible on fresh specimens. This subtle pink trimming sets it apart from other yellow sulphur butterflies, making it one of the more elegantly dressed members of its family.
description: The pink-edged sulphur is a medium-sized butterfly with bright yellow wings decorated with a distinctive pink border. This beautiful butterfly is actually Maine's official state butterfly, representing the rugged beauty of northern New England. Adults typically have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches, with males usually displaying more vibrant coloring than females. Like other sulphur butterflies, they're active fliers that seem to dance through meadows and forest openings on sunny days.

idTips.label: Pink wing borders
idTips.description: Look for the telltale rosy-pink edging along the wing margins - this is most vivid on fresh butterflies and can appear almost coral-colored when the light hits it just right

idTips.label: Bright yellow base color
idTips.description: The wings show a rich, buttery yellow that's more intense than pale sulphurs but not as orange-tinted as some relatives

idTips.label: Dark wing borders
idTips.description: Males have solid black borders on the forewings, while females show more broken or spotted dark edging with yellow spots mixed in

idTips.label: Wing underside pattern
idTips.description: The undersides are paler yellow-green with a silvery spot rimmed in pink on the hindwings - visible when the butterfly lands with wings folded

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a bouncing, erratic pattern close to the ground, often stopping to nectar at low flowers where you can get a closer look

habitat: Pink-edged sulphurs prefer cooler, northern habitats including forest clearings, meadows, and bog edges throughout New England's mountains and northern regions. They're particularly fond of areas where blueberries and other heath family plants grow, as these serve as host plants for their caterpillars. You're most likely to spot them in partially shaded openings rather than wide-open sunny fields.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with fresh butterflies showing the most vibrant pink wing borders. This is an excellent time for identification as the colors are at their peak.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight period runs through June and July when adults are most active and numerous. Look for mating pairs and egg-laying females near blueberry bushes.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may appear in late summer through early September, though these butterflies often show more faded coloring. By late fall, all adults have died and the species overwinters as pupae.
seasonality.winter: No adults are visible - the species survives winter in the pupal stage, tucked away in protective cocoons among leaf litter and low vegetation.

funFact: Despite being Maine's official state butterfly, pink-edged sulphurs are actually quite rare and localized - you're more likely to see Maine's state bird (the chickadee) than its state butterfly, making every sighting a special treat for nature watchers!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with clouded sulphurs and orange sulphurs, but the pink wing edges are the dead giveaway - neither of those species has this rosy trim. Memory trick: 'Pink edges make it special' - if you see pink borders on a yellow butterfly in New England, you've found something uncommon.
contextualKnowledge: As Maine's state butterfly, the pink-edged sulphur was chosen to represent the state's commitment to preserving its unique northern ecosystems, though ironically this honor has brought attention to how rarely most people actually encounter this beautiful but elusive species.
compareHints: Unlike its common cousins the clouded sulphur and orange sulphur, the pink-edged sulphur prefers cooler, more northern habitats and is much less frequently seen. While clouded sulphurs are bright yellow with black borders and orange sulphurs show orange patches, only the pink-edged sulphur displays those distinctive rosy-pink wing edges. The pink-edged sulphur is also generally smaller and more delicate-looking than its more robust relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Clouded Sulphurs are pure lemon-yellow without the orange tinge of Orange Sulphurs, and they're much more common at lower elevations than Pink-edged Sulphurs.
Orange Sulphurs are distinguished from their closest relative, the Clouded Sulphur, by their distinctive orange glow, particularly in males, while Clouded Sulphurs remain a paler lemon-yellow.
